title: Young Morgan Band and Transcena's banjo test at Spanish Fort
summary: A story of the boss Transcena sitting by banjo players and firing one, and how Vincent survived by chording up the neck.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: And ask him if you ever worked with the Young Morgan Band.

Have you ever worked with the Young Morgan Band? Yeah, yeah. Let me see. Isaiah Martin. Yeah, I used to work with him. He played his band. He played for me. He was playing out at Spanish Post. And you know, old man, Transcena, he could play music too. Transcena, that's the fella who used to run the place out there, you know. You know what I was talking about? Transcena? That was the boss, you know, who used to run that, you know, that place out there. But anyhow, he was a great bass fella. He didn't sit in the chair like you said. He turned the chair on his chair and hold it up. So one night, he was sitting there looking at Joe, you know, playing banjo. And Joe is sitting down, there's a plane. So Joe says, guy can't play no banjo with me. This guy can't play no banjo with me. There he goes. So we asked him why the boss come back and sit at him. He said, let me see that banjo. Joe Hennington, you know. He said, hey boy, play too. And they played, no man played. He was so surprised. He didn't know what to do. He said, you don't play nothing. He said, ticka, ticka, ticka, ticka, ticka, ticka. Run all up and down. I said, you don't make no calls. You don't say, ticka, ticka, ticka, ticka. So they fired him. And when they got me, they said, Dad, I just began to rag, I got you. He said, Dad, open them ears. I wasn't ready. I was saying, he said, cause the boss played music. And he's gonna sit right by you and listen to it. And if you don't, if you're good enough, he's gonna take it away and play himself and show you. I got that. It made me nervous, you know. I got, I got scared, you know, like that. I don't know what he's doing. So they come, that night, the first night, they had all our music. That was Celestane's job. Celestane turned it over to Lewis Tameen, you know. And Lewis Tameen had me with him then. So when we played a tune, after we played two tunes, he said he'd come sit by me, just like he'd sit by me. And the way I survived, after we played about four or five tunes, he got up and then he left. He didn't say nothing, you know. He said, well, he said nothing yet, Papa Dad. He said, we don't know what's worth, but we hope you like your playing. He said, see, I could make all them chords all the time. Wouldn't have to slide my hand down. I said, I like, you know. And if you didn't do all that, you know, ooh, ooh, ooh, you wasn't in the line, you see. You can't play. I could make all my chords all up there, make change, everything. Mine, seven, ninth chord, everything all up in the day. I'd get down there and make it the same way. Wouldn't have to slide my hand, you know. Then sometime when I want to take a little hop, you know, get there like that side. That's why some of the banjo players didn't like my playing, you know. But they know I could chord. I tell them, if anybody can play, I can play with it. But if you can't play, I say, I can't play with you. I say, because I be playing right, you be playing wrong, makes everything sound bad, you know.
